title: Primordial Black Holes as Cosmic Architects: Imprints of an extended mass function
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures + 4 pages appendix. Submitted for publication to ApJ
summary: Primordial black holes (PBHs) remain compelling dark-matter candidates and possible relics of early-Universe physics, with observable imprints across both cosmological structure formation and gravitational-wave astronomy. We investigate the consequences of a PBH population described by an extended, physically motivated mass function shaped by features in the thermal history of the early Universe. We compute the associated Poisson contribution to the matter power spectrum and propagate its effects to the halo mass function, the cosmic star-formation rate density, and the reionization history. The PBH component produces a moderate enhancement of small-scale power, leading to earlier low-mass halo formation and a correspondingly mild increase in the high-redshift star-formation rate density while remaining consistent with current constraints on the Thomson optical depth. We then evaluate the merger-rate distribution expected for current and future gravitational-wave detectors. In the stellar-mass regime, the predicted PBH binary population occupies the region probed by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA and can contribute to the observed compact-object merger population. For LISA, the detectable signal is dominated by intermediate-mass binaries with component masses of $10^3$-$10^4\,M_\odot$, with cumulative rates of order a few events per year extending to redshifts as high as $z \sim 50$. The detection of such high-redshift intermediate-mass black hole mergers would constitute a distinctive signature of a primordial origin, providing evidence that PBHs contribute non-negligibly to the dark matter budget and may have served as early seeds for the supermassive black holes observed at later cosmic epochs.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates extended-mass-function primordial black holes (PBHs) shaped by early-Universe thermal history, computing their effects on matter power spectrum, halo formation, star formation, and reionization. It finds moderate small-scale power enhancement and predicts merger rates detectable by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (stellar-mass) and LISA (intermediate-mass 10^3–10^4 M⊙ binaries, a few events/year up to z~50), identifying high-redshift IMBH mergers as distinctive signatures of primordial origin.
AI.motivation: To determine whether PBHs with a physically motivated extended mass function can account for dark matter and produce observable signatures across cosmological structure formation and gravitational-wave astronomy, while remaining consistent with existing constraints.
AI.method: The authors model a PBH population with an extended mass function derived from features in early-Universe thermal history. They also evaluate PBH binary merger-rate distributions for current (LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA) and future (LISA) gravitational-wave detectors.

Stellar-mass PBH binaries overlap with the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observed merger population. For LISA, intermediate-mass binaries (10^3–10^4 M⊙) dominate, with cumulative rates of a few events per year up to z~50.
AI.conclusion: Detection of high-redshift intermediate-mass black hole mergers would be a distinctive signature of primordial origin, indicating PBHs contribute non-negligibly to the dark matter budget and may have seeded the supermassive black holes observed at later cosmic epochs.

title: Assembly bias from nuisance to probe II: Salvaging linear clustering from DESI and SDSS data
summary: Galactic conformity links the properties of neighbouring galaxies and is usually interpreted as a signature of assembly-biased galaxy occupation. We study projected and redshift-space compensated conformity statistics in colour-selected DESI BGS and SDSS MGS samples. These combine correlations of related galaxy populations, suppressing shared nonlinear clustering contributions while retaining a differential large-scale response. We test whether this exposes the linear matter correlation-function shape where ordinary colour-selected clustering has a scale-dependent nonlinear response. We split galaxies into red and blue subsamples and measure ordinary correlations, conformity, and compensated combinations in projection and redshift-space monopoles, using central primaries by default. We fit linear matter templates, diagnose the response with effective kernels, and compare with MTNG, FLAMINGO, and MDPL2--SAG. Ordinary high-colour clustering broadly follows the linear templates but develops a scale-dependent small-scale response. In DESI, $Δf_0(s)$, projected $Δf(r_p)$, and $C_w(r_p)$ track the linear matter shape substantially further into the nonlinear regime, consistent with suppression of nonlinear clustering modes while leaving a linear-matter-like mode visible. The effect is stronger for central-primary and dense samples. Projected effective kernels are enhanced at low line-of-sight separations, helping the residual resemble $ξ_{\rm mm}^{\rm lin}(r_p)$ rather than $w_{\rm mm}^{\rm lin}(r_p)$. Simulations reproduce the qualitative behaviour with model-dependent amplitudes and residual scale dependence. These results suggest that assembly-sensitive population differences can filter nonlinear clustering modes, although surviving nonlinear contamination must be calibrated before precision cosmological use. (abridged)

The authors aim to test whether galactic conformity—usually interpreted as assembly bias—combined with compensated statistics can suppress shared nonlinear clustering modes and expose the linear matter correlation-function shape for potential precision cosmological use.
AI.method: Galaxies are split into red and blue subsamples. Ordinary correlations, conformity, and compensated combinations are measured in projection and redshift-space monopoles using central primaries. Linear matter templates are fit, effective kernels diagnose the response, and comparisons are made with MTNG, FLAMINGO, and MDPL2–SAG simulations.
AI.result: Ordinary high-colour clustering broadly follows linear templates but develops scale-dependent small-scale response. In DESI, the compensated statistics (Δf0(s), projected Δf(rp), and C_w(rp)) track the linear matter shape further into the nonlinear regime, consistent with suppression of nonlinear modes. Effects are stronger for central-primary and dense samples. Projected effective kernels are enhanced at low line-of-sight separations, making the residual resemble ξ_mm^lin(rp) rather than w_mm^lin(rp). Simulations reproduce qualitative behaviour with model-dependent amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: Assembly-sensitive population differences can filter nonlinear clustering modes, but surviving nonlinear contamination requires calibration before precision cosmological application.

title: $\texttt{SPINE}$: Symbolic Models to Predict the Evolution of the $Λ$CDM Nonlinear Power Spectrum
summary: We present $\texttt{SPINE}$ and $\texttt{SPINEX}$, a pair of analytical emulators developed to predict the nonlinear power spectrum based on its linear counterpart and several essential cosmological parameters within the range of $0.01\;h\;\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1} <k< 2\;h\;\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1} $. The primary difference between the two models is their parameterisation. Our methodology is grounded in the mapping originally proposed by Peacock and Dodds (1996). Both models are defined by clear mathematical expressions derived from symbolic regression, a machine learning technique that utilises genetic programming to identify analytical equations that accurately represent the underlying data. This approach provides a more interpretable and efficient alternative to conventional numerical methods that should also exhibit superior extrapolation behaviour beyond the training range. The emulators have been trained on the $Λ$CDM Quijote Latin Hypercube simulations. We provide fits for both emulators across three distinct scenarios: cosmologies within 20$σ$ of the Planck-2018 observations, a designated fiducial cosmology, and a broader range of cosmologies sampled from the Quijote simulations. Our findings indicate that $\texttt{SPINE}$ and $\texttt{SPINEX}$ maintain an accuracy of better than 5% in the majority of cases. These emulators provide a rapid alternative to numerical methods, and future initiatives will focus on developing expressions that incorporate galaxy bias and redshift-space distortions. This advancement aims to enhance the modelling of redshift space power spectra across multiple redshifts, enabling their application in large-scale cosmological surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SPINE and SPINEX, two analytical emulators that predict the nonlinear matter power spectrum from its linear counterpart and cosmological parameters across 0.01–2 h/Mpc. Built on symbolic regression (genetic programming) and the Peacock-Dodds mapping, they provide interpretable analytical expressions trained on Quijote ΛCDM simulations, achieving better than 5% accuracy and offering a fast, extrapolative alternative to numerical methods.
AI.motivation: To provide interpretable and efficient analytical emulators for predicting the nonlinear power spectrum, offering a more transparent and rapidly computable alternative to conventional numerical approaches that may also extrapolate better beyond the training range.
AI.method: The method uses symbolic regression, a genetic-programming-based machine learning technique, to derive closed-form analytical expressions. It is grounded in the Peacock-Dodds (1996) mapping between linear and nonlinear power spectra. Two models (SPINE and SPINEX) differ in parameterisation and are trained on the ΛCDM Quijote Latin Hypercube simulations, with fits provided for three cosmological scenarios around Planck-2018 constraints.
AI.result: Both emulators achieve better than 5% accuracy in most cases across wavenumbers 0.01–2 h/Mpc for multiple cosmological scenarios (20σ of Planck-2018, fiducial, and broader Quijote-sampled cosmologies). They provide rapid predictions compared to numerical methods.
AI.conclusion: SPINE and SPINEX are fast, accurate analytical emulators for nonlinear power spectrum prediction. Future work will extend the framework to include galaxy bias and redshift-space distortions for modelling redshift-space power spectra at multiple redshifts for large-scale cosmological surveys.

title: The host galaxies of 2003fg-like type Ia supernovae
summary: SN~2003fg-like events are a peculiar type Ia supernova (SN~Ia) subtype characterized by broader light curves, higher near-infrared luminosities, and stronger carbon absorptions at early times. Here we present observations of the largest compilation of 2003fg-like SN Ia host galaxies to date, obtained with Integral Field Spectroscopy (IFS). For 20 objects, we study both the global host-galaxy properties and, for the first time for a sizeable sample, the local environment at the SN position. Globally, 2003fg-like SNe~Ia occur in galaxies with lower stellar mass, lower oxygen abundance, and marginally higher specific star-formation rate (sSFR) than those of normal SNe~Ia, although their hosts are not as extreme in such properties as superluminous SNe, nor representative of metal-poor dwarf-galaxy samples. Locally, the SN positions show lower star-formation-rate, stellar-mass surface densities, and lower sSFR, than normal SN~Ia environments, consistent with a significant preference for the outskirts of their hosts, while their stellar age indicators are typical. The most distinctive local property is metallicity, with 2003fg-like SNe~Ia occupying the most metal-poor environments among SNe~Ia. We also find a tentative positive correlation between the light-curve width and the oxygen abundance for 2003fg-like events. Our results imply that 2003fg-like SNe~Ia arise from the merger of two white dwarfs (WDs) or the core-degenerate scenario, but disfavor the single, rapidly rotating super-M$_{ch}$ C-O WD progenitor, as this channel requires a young stellar population that we do not observe at the SN positions. The preference of 2003fg-like SNe~Ia for low-metallicity environments suggests that they may have been more common in the early Universe. (abridged)

Their progenitor channel is favored to be double white-dwarf mergers or core-degenerate scenarios, disfavoring the single super-Chandrasekhar rapidly-rotating WD path, and they may have been more common in the early Universe.
AI.motivation: To understand the progenitor systems and environmental preferences of the peculiar 2003fg-like SN Ia subtype, which is rare and poorly understood. While global host properties have been studied, the local environment at the SN position had not been systematically investigated for a sizeable sample before this work.
AI.method: Integral Field Spectroscopy (IFS) observations of 20 2003fg-like SN Ia host galaxies. The authors analyze both global host-galaxy properties (stellar mass, oxygen abundance, specific star-formation rate) and local environment properties at the SN positions (star-formation rate, stellar-mass surface densities, sSFR, stellar age, metallicity), comparing them to normal SNe Ia and other SN subtypes.

Locally, SN positions show lower SFR, stellar-mass surface densities, and sSFR than normal SN Ia environments, with a preference for host outskirts; stellar age indicators are typical. The most distinctive local property is metallicity: 2003fg-like SNe Ia occupy the most metal-poor environments among SNe Ia. A tentative positive correlation between light-curve width and oxygen abundance is found.
AI.conclusion: The results support a double white-dwarf merger or core-degenerate scenario for 2003fg-like SNe Ia, while disfavoring the single rapidly rotating super-Mch C-O WD progenitor because that channel requires a young stellar population not observed at the SN positions. The preference for low-metallicity environments suggests 2003fg-like SNe Ia may have been more common in the early Universe.

title: Scatter, bias, and chaos of satellite orbits in triaxial dark matter haloes
summary: The pericentric distances of satellite galaxies govern their tidal stripping, quenching, and survival, yet their orbits are almost universally computed in spherical host potentials, whereas dark matter haloes are generically triaxial. We quantify, orbit by orbit, the error this simplification incurs. We integrate $10^6$ satellites, drawn from a cosmological infall distribution, in static NFW hosts of systematically varying triaxiality at fixed mass profile. Triaxiality leaves the population medians of pericentre, apocentre, and orbital period essentially unchanged. Instead, successive pericentres of an individual orbit scatter by 5-23% depending on host shape, irrespective of orbital energy; the minimum pericentre distance reached within a Hubble time shrinks systematically by up to 21%, enhancing the peak tidal mass loss. This triaxiality-driven orbital dephasing is overwhelmingly regular rather than chaotic; chaotic satellite orbits are common and dominate the near-centre pericentric passages in strongly flattened hosts, but diverge on time-scales far exceeding the Hubble time. Satellite orbits spherically reconstructed via direct backward integration in a truly triaxial host diverge by a tenth of the virial radius within 2-4 Gyr, with comparable uncertainties sourced separately by the unconstrained shape of the host and by its unknown absolute orientation. For the Milky Way dwarf Triangulum II, the unknown halo shape and orientation alone spread the inferred pericentre by ~50%, five times its reported uncertainty and more than ten times the LMC-induced shift, and bias it by 6-70%. This host-shape uncertainty can dominate satellite orbital error budgets and should be incorporated in future inferences.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies the error incurred by computing satellite galaxy orbits in spherical host potentials when real dark matter haloes are triaxial. Using 10^6 integrated satellites in triaxial NFW hosts, the authors find triaxiality leaves population medians of pericentre/apocentre/period unchanged but causes 5-23% scatter in successive pericentres, shrinks minimum pericentre by up to 21%, and causes orbital dephasing that is mostly regular (not chaotic). Spherically reconstructed orbits diverge by a tenth of the virial radius within 2-4 Gyr. For the Milky Way dwarf Triangulum II, unknown halo shape and orientation spread the inferred pericentre by ~50%, far exceeding reported uncertainties.
AI.motivation: Satellite galaxy orbits govern tidal stripping, quenching, and survival, but are almost universally computed assuming spherical host potentials, whereas dark matter haloes are generically triaxial. The magnitude of the error this simplification introduces has not been systematically quantified.
AI.method: The authors integrate 10^6 satellites drawn from a cosmological infall distribution in static NFW hosts with systematically varying triaxiality at fixed mass profile. They analyze orbit-by-orbit errors in pericentre, apocentre, orbital period, and tidal mass loss, examine whether the resulting orbital dephasing is regular or chaotic, test spherical reconstruction via direct backward integration, and apply the uncertainty framework to the Milky Way dwarf Triangulum II.
AI.result: Triaxiality leaves population medians essentially unchanged but introduces 5-23% scatter in successive pericentres regardless of orbital energy; minimum pericentre within a Hubble time shrinks by up to 21%, enhancing peak tidal mass loss. The dephasing is overwhelmingly regular rather than chaotic (chaotic orbits diverge on timescales far exceeding the Hubble time). Spherically reconstructed orbits diverge by a tenth of the virial radius within 2-4 Gyr, with comparable uncertainties from unknown host shape and orientation. For Triangulum II, unknown halo shape/orientation spread the inferred pericentre by ~50%, five times its reported uncertainty and over ten times the LMC-induced shift, biasing it by 6-70%.
AI.conclusion: Host-shape uncertainty can dominate satellite orbital error budgets and should be incorporated in future inferences of satellite orbits and their derived properties.

title: Paleo-Detectors as a Novel Probe of Dark Matter-Nucleus Effective Interactions
summary: Paleo-detectors are a proposed approach to the direct detection of dark matter (DM) based on the observation of DM-induced nuclear recoils. Rather than relying on large detector masses required for conventional detectors, paleo-detectors exploit extremely long integration times, using small samples of naturally occurring minerals that have resided deep underground and accumulated damage tracks over geological timescales of order a gigayear. In this contribution, we review recent theoretical predictions for the sensitivity of paleo-detectors to WIMP-nucleus interactions within the framework of a Non-Relativistic Effective Field Theory (NREFT). We discuss both elastic and inelastic scattering processes and consider isoscalar couplings, taking into account backgrounds from neutrinos and radiogenic sources. We present projected sensitivities of paleo-detectors for different readout and exposure scenarios and compare the reach of paleo-detectors to that of conventional direct-detection experiments. For DM masses in the range $1\ \mathrm{GeV}/c^2$-$10\ \mathrm{GeV}/c^2$, paleo-detectors are expected to achieve sensitivities exceeding those of conventional experiments for WIMP-nucleus interactions mediated by all NREFT operators, with only a weak dependence on the read-out scenario or target mineral. For larger DM masses, $10\ \mathrm{GeV}/c^2$-$5\ \mathrm{TeV}/c^2$, paleo-detectors are projected to attain sensitivities comparable to or surpassing conventional experiments for interactions mediated by several NREFT operators, depending on the specific read-out scenario and choice of target mineral.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews theoretical projections for paleo-detectors—a proposed approach to dark matter detection using ancient minerals that accumulated nuclear recoil damage tracks over gigayear timescales—within the Non-Relativistic Effective Field Theory (NREFT) framework. It covers elastic and inelastic WIMP-nucleus scattering with isoscalar couplings, considers neutrino and radiogenic backgrounds, and finds that for DM masses of 1–10 GeV/c², paleo-detectors exceed conventional experiment sensitivities for all NREFT operators, while for 10 GeV/c²–5 TeV/c², they achieve comparable or superior sensitivity for several operators depending on readout and target mineral choices.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to exploit the extremely long integration times (~gigayear) of naturally occurring minerals deep underground as a novel approach to dark matter direct detection, since paleo-detectors can accumulate DM-induced nuclear recoil damage over geological timescales, potentially overcoming the sensitivity limitations of conventional detectors that require large masses.
AI.method: The authors review theoretical sensitivity projections for paleo-detectors within the NREFT framework, considering both elastic and inelastic WIMP-nucleus scattering with isoscalar couplings. They incorporate backgrounds from neutrinos and radiogenic sources, and evaluate sensitivities across different readout scenarios and exposure configurations, comparing the projected reach against conventional direct-detection experiments.
AI.result: For DM masses in 1–10 GeV/c², paleo-detectors are projected to achieve sensitivities exceeding conventional experiments for WIMP-nucleus interactions mediated by all NREFT operators, with weak dependence on readout scenario or target mineral. For 10 GeV/c²–5 TeV/c², paleo-detectors attain sensitivities comparable to or better than conventional experiments for several NREFT operators, depending on the specific readout and target mineral configuration.
AI.conclusion: Paleo-detectors represent a promising complementary approach to dark matter direct detection, particularly advantageous for low-mass WIMPs (1–10 GeV/c²) where their sensitivity uniformly surpasses conventional detectors across all NREFT operators, while for higher masses their competitive reach depends on the NREFT operator, readout scheme, and target mineral selection.

title: Barren but not Empty: The Impact of Void Environments on Galaxy and Halo Populations
summary: The combination of gravitational collapse and an accelerating expansion of the Universe drive an increasing fraction of volume toward becoming low-density voids across cosmic time. These regions present a unique environment due to their low density, which leads to them behaving similarly to "pocket universes" with modified cosmological parameters. Since the formation and evolution of galaxies is strongly tied to the environment, we aim to discern how voids alter halos and galaxies compared to the general population in the universe. We use the hydrodynamical cosmological simulation suite Magneticum Pathfinder and introduce a set of void halo mass functions (VHMFs), which trace the halo population as a function of void-centric distance. We find galactic halos in voids to be overall less massive than in the general simulation volume. This discrepancy between void and field halos evolves with time as the voids grow more underdense, while the populations are still very similar at cosmic dawn. Expanding on this, we evaluate whether specific properties of the voids affect the VHMFs. We find the only relevant parameter for the void halo population to be the core density, a measure of the strength of underdensity. To assess the impact of the density environment on the evolution of galaxies, we investigate whether there are any distinctions between void and field galaxies with regard to stellar properties. We compute the stellar-mass function, halo mass-stellar mass relation, as well as the star-forming main sequence using the same void-centric shells. Although voids contain overall less stellar mass, the distribution of galaxies along the stellar mass-halo mass follows that of other regions. This implies that SF proceeded "conventionally" in void regions, in agreement with more recent observations.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the Magneticum Pathfinder hydrodynamical simulation suite to study how cosmic voids alter halo and galaxy properties compared to the general field population. It introduces void halo mass functions (VHMFs) as a function of void-centric distance, finding void halos are less massive and this discrepancy grows over time. Only the core density of voids affects the halo population. While void galaxies contain less stellar mass, they follow conventional star formation scaling relations.
AI.motivation: Since the formation and evolution of galaxies is strongly tied to environment, the authors aim to discern how voids—low-density regions behaving like "pocket universes" with modified cosmological parameters—alter halos and galaxies compared to the general population in the universe.
AI.method: The authors use the hydrodynamical cosmological simulation suite Magneticum Pathfinder and introduce a set of void halo mass functions (VHMFs) that trace the halo population as a function of void-centric distance. They compute stellar-mass functions, halo mass-stellar mass relations, and the star-forming main sequence across the same void-centric shells.
AI.result: Galactic halos in voids are overall less massive than in the general simulation volume, a discrepancy that evolves with time as voids become more underdense, while populations are similar at cosmic dawn. The only relevant void parameter affecting VHMFs is core density. Although voids contain less stellar mass, the distribution along the stellar mass-halo mass relation follows that of other regions, implying conventional star formation in voids.
AI.conclusion: Void environment suppresses halo masses relative to the field, with the effect strengthening as voids grow more underdense. However, star formation proceeded "conventionally" within void regions despite lower stellar masses, consistent with recent observational findings.

title: The Impact of Magnitude Uncertainties and K-corrections on Standard Siren Measurements of the Hubble Constant
summary: Gravitational-wave standard sirens provide an independent probe of the Hubble constant. Dark siren analyses that rely on galaxy catalogues are sensitive to catalogue-related uncertainties. While incompleteness, weighting schemes, and redshift errors have been studied extensively, the impact of magnitude uncertainties and K-corrections has received little attention so far. We assess how magnitude errors and K-corrections propagate into the Hubble constant inference, and compare their impact to that of realistic spectroscopic redshift errors to determine their relevance. We use a modified version of the gwcosmo Python package to construct line-of-sight redshift priors from a complete, volume-limited mock galaxy catalogue up to $z<0.2$. We simulate and analyse a sample of $\sim200$ binary black hole events with luminosity weighting in the $B$- and $K$-bands and test different uncertainty models for redshifts, magnitudes, and K-corrections. The choice of luminosity-weighting scheme has a substantial impact on the inferred Hubble constant posterior, with the direct $B$- and $K$-band comparison producing differences comparable to the largest uncertainty-induced changes. Spectroscopic redshift errors produce the largest integrated changes in the Hubble constant posterior among the tested uncertainty treatments. Photometric magnitude uncertainties lead to substantially smaller, band-dependent deviations. In the $K$-band, the tested K-correction treatments have only a minor impact in the present low-redshift mock analysis, with the empirical correction slightly reducing the integrated deviation relative to the no-correction case. In realistic, flux-limited catalogues with larger localization areas and photometric or mixed redshift errors, the relative impact of magnitude uncertainties is expected to be even smaller, indicating that they need not be prioritized in near-future dark siren analyses.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates how magnitude uncertainties and K-corrections propagate into Hubble constant (H0) inference from gravitational-wave dark siren analyses, using simulated binary black hole events and a volume-limited mock galaxy catalogue (z<0.2). It finds spectroscopic redshift errors dominate the H0 posterior impact, while magnitude uncertainties produce smaller band-dependent deviations and K-correction effects are minor, concluding that magnitude-related uncertainties need not be prioritized in near-future dark siren analyses.
AI.motivation: While incompleteness, weighting schemes, and redshift errors in dark siren galaxy-catalogue-based H0 measurements have been extensively studied, the impact of magnitude uncertainties and K-corrections has received little attention. This work aims to quantify their relevance relative to realistic spectroscopic redshift errors to determine whether they warrant prioritization in future analyses.
AI.method: The authors modify the gwcosmo Python package to construct line-of-sight redshift priors from a complete, volume-limited mock galaxy catalogue up to z<0.2. They simulate and analyze ~200 binary black hole events with B- and K-band luminosity weighting, testing different uncertainty models for redshifts, magnitudes, and K-corrections to assess their propagation into the Hubble constant posterior.
AI.result: The choice of luminosity-weighting scheme has a substantial impact on the inferred H0 posterior, with direct B- and K-band comparison producing differences comparable to the largest uncertainty-induced changes. Spectroscopic redshift errors cause the largest integrated posterior changes, while photometric magnitude uncertainties yield substantially smaller, band-dependent deviations. K-corrections have minor impact in the low-redshift mock analysis, with the empirical correction slightly reducing deviation. In realistic flux-limited scenarios with larger localizations and photometric/mixed redshift errors, magnitude uncertainty impact is expected to be even smaller.
AI.conclusion: Magnitude uncertainties and K-corrections are secondary to redshift errors in influencing dark siren H0 inferences and need not be prioritized in near-future analyses, with redshift error treatment and luminosity-weighting scheme choice being the more critical systematic considerations.

title: A Broken Clock Is Right Twice a Day: [Ce/Mg] Is Not a Universal Chemical Clock
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures; submitted to AAS journals
summary: The ratio of $s$-process to $α$-element enrichment ($[s/α]$) has been proposed as a ``chemical clock,'' or a means to estimate stellar ages. However, the age--$[s/α]$ relation varies with metallicity and location in the Galaxy, and the observed trends are not well predicted by galactic chemical evolution models. We quantify the age--[Ce/Mg] correlation across the Galactic disk in roughly 100,000 red giant stars observed with APOGEE in the SDSS-V Milky Way Mapper survey. We find that the slope of the correlation varies significantly with metallicity and guiding radius in the chemical thin disk. The trend is steepest in the outer disk and below Solar metallicity, while the most metal-rich stars and those in the inner disk show no correlation with age. In contrast, [Ce/Mg] patterns in the chemical thick disk are consistent across the Galaxy. Halo stars have higher [Ce/Mg] than the chemical thick disk, suggesting that asymptotic giant branch (AGB) enrichment is important even at low metallicity. Overall, patterns in [Ce/Mg] trace both the local star formation history and AGB nucleosynthesis. The complex interplay between [Ce/Mg], age, metallicity, and Galactic position means that [Ce/Mg] (and by extension $[s/α]$) is not a universal chemical clock.

AI.tldr: Using ~100,000 APOGEE red giant stars, this paper shows that the [Ce/Mg] age correlation (a proposed chemical clock) varies significantly with metallicity and Galactic position, is consistent only in the thick disk, and is not a universal chemical clock.
AI.motivation: The [s/α] enrichment ratio has been proposed as a chemical clock for estimating stellar ages, but the age–[s/α] relation varies with metallicity and Galactic location, and is not well predicted by galactic chemical evolution models. This paper aims to quantify these variations to assess the reliability of this chemical clock.
AI.method: The authors analyze roughly 100,000 red giant stars observed with APOGEE in the SDSS-V Milky Way Mapper survey, quantifying the age–[Ce/Mg] correlation across the Galactic disk. They examine how the slope of this correlation varies as a function of metallicity and guiding radius, and compare patterns across the chemical thin disk, thick disk, and halo.
AI.result: The age–[Ce/Mg] slope varies significantly with metallicity and guiding radius in the chemical thin disk: steepest in the outer disk and below Solar metallicity, while no correlation is found for the most metal-rich stars and inner disk stars. Thick disk [Ce/Mg] patterns are consistent across the Galaxy, and halo stars show higher [Ce/Mg] than the thick disk, indicating AGB enrichment is important even at low metallicity.
AI.conclusion: [Ce/Mg] (and by extension [s/α]) is not a universal chemical clock due to the complex interplay between [Ce/Mg], age, metallicity, and Galactic position. The observed patterns trace both local star formation history and AGB nucleosynthesis.

title: HOLISMOKES -- XVIII. Cosmology with strongly lensed type II supernovae: Effects of instrumental setups on $H_0$
summary: The upcoming Rubin Observatory and subsequent follow-up observations should improve the determination of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) via time-delay cosmography of strongly lensed type II supernovae (LSNe II), by enabling the detection of many more such events. In our previous work, we developed a method for determining the supernova (SN) phase from spectral absorption features. Because obtaining spectra of faint targets such as distant SN II is expensive, we examined how low-resolution spectra influence the precision of time-delay retrieval, and consequently the precision on $H_0$. We considered spectral resolutions $R = \fracλ{Δλ}$ between 100 and 250, and we investigated three signal-to-noise ratio ($S/N$) values of 10, 15, and 20, for each resolution. Furthermore, we forecast the precision on $H_{0}$ achievable with $S/N=10$ and compared the observing time required to reach it with ground-based and space-based facilities. We find that the time delay can be determined without bias and with uncertainties as low as 1.3 days for the investigated resolutions and $S/N$ values when we combine time-delay measurements of multiple absorption lines. For a typical LSN II system (absolute magnitude $\sim-$17 mag in the rest-frame V band, source redshift of \zs = 0.8), the required exposure times range from multiple hours for ground-based observations to a few minutes for space-based observations with the JWST. Our predictions on the precision of $H_0$ for a single lensed SN range from 14.2\% for $R = 100$ and $S/N$ = 10 to 7.5\% for $R = 250$ and $S/N$ = 20, enabling a 1\% determination of $H_0$ from $\sim$20 lensed SNe in the coming years.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how low-resolution spectra (R=100-250) and signal-to-noise ratios (S/N=10, 15, 20) affect the precision of time-delay measurements and Hubble constant determination from strongly lensed Type II supernovae. The authors find unbiased time-delay determination with uncertainties as low as 1.3 days, achieving H0 precision ranging from 14.2% to 7.5% per lensed SN, with ~20 events needed for a 1% H0 determination.
AI.motivation: With the upcoming Rubin Observatory enabling detection of many more strongly lensed Type II supernovae (LSNe II), time-delay cosmography can improve H0 determination. However, spectral follow-up of faint distant SN II is expensive, so the authors aim to determine how low-resolution, low-S/N spectra affect the precision of time-delay retrieval and consequently the precision on H0.
AI.method: The authors use their previously developed method of determining SN phase from spectral absorption features. They investigate spectral resolutions R between 100 and 250 and three S/N values (10, 15, 20) for each resolution. They combine time-delay measurements from multiple absorption lines and forecast H0 precision for S/N=10, comparing required observing times across ground-based and space-based (JWST) facilities.
AI.result: Time delay can be determined without bias with uncertainties as low as 1.3 days across the investigated resolutions and S/N values. For a typical LSN II system (absolute magnitude ~-17 mag in rest-frame V, source redshift 0.8), exposure times range from hours (ground-based) to minutes (JWST). Predicted H0 precision per lensed SN ranges from 14.2% (R=100, S/N=10) to 7.5% (R=250, S/N=20), enabling 1% H0 determination from ~20 lensed SNe.
AI.conclusion: Low-resolution spectra are sufficient for precise time-delay cosmography of LSNe II, and the combination of multiple absorption lines yields robust unbiased measurements. With the Rubin Observatory's detection capabilities, approximately 20 lensed SNe II could enable a 1% determination of H0 in the coming years, with JWST providing efficient follow-up observations for faint targets.

title: The origin of the stellar mass-size relation of satellite galaxies in the COLIBRE simulations
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: We study the stellar mass-size relation of satellite galaxies in the COLIBRE suite of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations. Satellites deviate from the relation that holds for centrals galaxies, where at the high mass end, $\log (M_*/{\rm M}_\odot) > 10.5$, sizes (defined as the 3D half-mass radius $r_{\rm h,*}$) increase systematically with mass ($r_{\rm h,*} \propto M_*^{0.5}$), whereas at lower masses, $8 < \log(M_*/{\rm M}_\odot) < 10.5$, the relation flattens and galaxy size becomes, on average, almost independent of mass ($r_{\rm h,*} \approx 3$ kpc). At $z=0$, dwarf satellites (defined as those with $8 < \log(M_*/{\rm M}_\odot) < 9$) are systematically larger than centrals of similar $M_*$. This trend reverses for bright satellites ($9 < \log(M_*/{\rm M}_\odot) < 10.5$), which are typically smaller than centrals of similar mass. We trace these trends to evolutionary processes affecting satellites after infall into the haloes of more massive hosts. At infall, dwarf satellites are typically gas-rich, dark matter-dominated systems with relatively large baryon-induced cores. These satellites quench rapidly after losing their gas to ram pressure, which prompts an immediate impulsive expansion due to the shallowing central potential, followed by secular expansion as their cored dark matter haloes are gradually stripped by tides. In contrast, the inner regions of bright satellites are baryon-dominated and resilient to tides. Centrally concentrated star formation increases their stellar mass, leading to smaller sizes and higher stellar metallicities (by $\approx 0.2$ dex) than those of centrals of similar mass. These distinct satellite evolutionary pathways lead to identifiable features in the mass-size-metallicity relations that may be compared with observations.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the stellar mass-size relation of satellite galaxies in the COLIBRE cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, finding that dwarf satellites are systematically larger than centrals while bright satellites are smaller, driven by distinct evolutionary processes after infall: dwarfs expand due to gas loss and tidal stripping of cored dark matter haloes, while bright satellites contract due to centrally concentrated star formation.
AI.motivation: To understand how satellite galaxies deviate from the stellar mass-size relation that holds for central galaxies, and to identify the physical mechanisms driving these deviations.
AI.method: Using the COLIBRE suite of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, the authors analyze the stellar mass-size relation (defined via 3D half-mass radius) of satellite galaxies at z=0, tracing their evolutionary history from infall, including effects of ram pressure stripping, tidal stripping, and star formation.
AI.result: At z=0, dwarf satellites (8 < log M*/M_sun < 9) are systematically larger than centrals of similar mass, while bright satellites (9 < log M*/M_sun < 10.5) are smaller. Dwarf satellites expand impulsively after ram-pressure-driven gas loss followed by secular expansion from tidal stripping of cored dark matter haloes; bright satellites shrink due to baryon-dominated inner regions resilient to tides and continued central star formation, also exhibiting higher stellar metallicities by ~0.2 dex.
AI.conclusion: Different satellite evolutionary pathways produce identifiable features in the mass-size-metallicity relations that can be compared with observational data to test and constrain models of satellite galaxy evolution.

title: Cross-simulator transfer with foundation model summaries: Towards robust SKA-era reionization inference
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, prepared for submission to A&A
summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) for parameter estimation is vulnerable to model misspecification: neural summaries and density estimators trained on a specific forward model typically fail when applied to data drawn from another model, or from real observations, and no training simulator can capture the full observational pipeline of a real measurement exactly. We show that a self-supervised Vision Transformer (ViT), pretrained label-free on a fast approximate simulator, produces transferable data summaries that generalize across simulators. Without retraining, it can be reused as a frozen encoder to infer astrophysical parameters from a completely different simulator that resolves the radiative transfer explicitly, on which it has never seen either data or parameters. As a concrete use case in 21cm cosmology, SKATR, a ViT pretrained with a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), serves as a foundation model for reionization inference from upcoming SKA measurements: SKATR is pretrained once on 67k low-cost, noiseless semi-numerical 21cmFAST lightcones, then frozen and applied to hydrodynamical Loreli II lightcones, where a lightweight conditional flow matching head infers five astrophysical parameters; the encoder is never shown Loreli data, its parameters, or any noise. In our comparison, SKATR yields the most precise and best-calibrated posteriors across all five parameters, matching the accuracy of the fully-supervised in-domain baseline while requiring 2.6x fewer radiative-transfer simulations. Under realistic SKA AA* noise, only SKATR remains simultaneously accurate, informative, and calibrated, outperforming even a supervised baseline retrained from scratch on noisy data. Self-supervised pretraining on computationally efficient semi-numerical simulations is therefore a viable route to calibrated, simulator- and noise-agnostic reionization inference for the SKA-era.

AI.tldr: SKATR, a self-supervised Vision Transformer pretrained on fast semi-numerical 21cmFAST simulations, serves as a frozen, transferable encoder for simulation-based inference of astrophysical parameters from completely different simulators (Loreli II) and noisy SKA data, yielding calibrated and accurate posteriors without ever seeing the target simulator's data or parameters.
AI.motivation: Simulation-based inference is vulnerable to model misspecification—neural summaries and density estimators trained on one forward model fail on data from other simulators or real observations, since no training simulator perfectly captures the real observational pipeline.
AI.method: Pretrain a Vision Transformer with Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) in a self-supervised, label-free manner on 67k low-cost, noiseless 21cmFAST lightcones. Then freeze this encoder and attach a lightweight conditional flow matching head to infer five astrophysical parameters from completely different hydrodynamical Loreli II lightcones—the encoder never sees Loreli data, its parameters, or any noise.
AI.result: SKATR produces the most precise and best-calibrated posteriors across all five parameters, matching the fully-supervised in-domain baseline accuracy while requiring 2.6x fewer radiative-transfer simulations. Under realistic SKA AA* noise, only SKATR remains simultaneously accurate, informative, and calibrated, even outperforming a supervised baseline retrained from scratch on noisy data.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining on computationally efficient semi-numerical simulations is a viable route to calibrated, simulator- and noise-agnostic reionization inference for the SKA era, demonstrating that frozen transferable encoders can overcome model misspecification in SBI.

title: Phase-Space Diagnostics for Dwarf Galaxies in Cluster Environments
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to ApJ, comments are welcome
summary: Ongoing effort is devoted to observing spectroscopic samples of dwarf galaxies in clusters, allowing the analysis of their distribution and associated trends in projected phase-space (PPS), i.e. line-of-sight velocity vs. projected clustercentric distance. By utilizing the resolved baryonic halos inside the galaxy clusters of a cosmological simulation from the Magneticum suite, we complement on prior studies with dedicated focus on the dwarf galaxy population ($M_\ast<10^9\,M_\odot$) and correlations between infall time and location in PPS. The inferred trend recovers the radial correlation reported by prior works, but we find a significant fraction ($\geq30\%$) of recently accreted galaxies at locations that were previously predicted to be dominated by ancient infallers. Splitting the diagram with an infall time threshold of 3 Gyr, we develop a detailed infall time template in PPS. We provide our data to allow observers to statistically infer the time of infall of their sample when placing them on the PPS. Additionally, we review the trajectories in PPS of different orbits and their dependence on the observer's orientation. Compared to massive galaxies, we find a much broader radial distribution for dwarfs in 3D PS. Utilizing a set of high-resolution idealized simulations, we predict strongly altered orbits for dark matter-deficient galaxies.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes the projected phase-space (PPS) distribution of dwarf galaxies in clusters using the Magneticum cosmological simulation, finding that at least 30% of recently accreted dwarfs occupy PPS regions previously thought to be dominated by ancient infallers. The authors develop a detailed infall-time template in PPS, provide their data for observers to statistically infer infall times, review orbit trajectories and their observer-orientation dependence, and use idealized simulations to predict strongly altered orbits for dark matter-deficient galaxies.
AI.motivation: To complement prior studies by providing dedicated analysis of the dwarf galaxy population (M*<10^9 M_sun) in clusters, specifically focusing on correlations between infall time and location in projected phase-space, and to provide observers with a template to statistically infer infall times of their samples.
AI.method: Using the resolved baryonic halos in galaxy clusters from the Magneticum cosmological simulation suite, the authors analyze the PPS distribution of dwarf galaxies and correlate it with infall time. They split the PPS using a 3 Gyr infall time threshold to build a template, review orbital trajectories and their dependence on observer orientation, and run high-resolution idealized simulations to examine orbits of dark matter-deficient galaxies.
AI.result: The study recovers the previously reported radial correlation in PPS but finds a significant fraction (≥30%) of recently accreted galaxies in regions previously predicted to be dominated by ancient infallers. Dwarf galaxies show a much broader radial distribution in 3D phase space compared to massive galaxies. Idealized simulations predict strongly altered orbits for dark matter-deficient galaxies.
AI.conclusion: Dwarf galaxy infall time cannot be uniquely inferred from PPS location alone due to significant contamination of recently accreted galaxies in ancient-infaller-dominated regions. The provided PPS infall-time template enables statistical inference of infall times for observational samples, while dark matter deficiency can substantially alter orbital behavior in clusters.

title: Revisiting the Hubble tension with an inverse power-law early dark energy
summary: We propose a new early dark energy with a potential that has an inverse power-law asymptotic tail to alleviate the Hubble tension. Fitting this model to the datasets of CMB+BAO+SN+H0DN, one obtains a 68$\%$ confidence-level value of $H_0\sim 70.20^{+0.60}_{-0.47}$ km s$^{-1}$Mpc$^{-1}$ and a best-fit value of $H_0\sim 70.56$ km s$^{-1}$Mpc$^{-1}$ for index $n=10$. We show that this model can be tested by future data of CMB and matter power spectra. Finally, we briefly discuss fine-tuning problems related to this model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new early dark energy model with an inverse power-law asymptotic tail in its potential to alleviate the Hubble tension. Fitting to CMB+BAO+SN+H0DN datasets yields H0 ~ 70.20 (+0.60/-0.47) km/s/Mpc at 68% CL (best-fit ~70.56 km/s/Mpc) for index n=10, with testability via future CMB and matter power spectrum data.
AI.motivation: To address the Hubble tension, the discrepancy between early-universe (CMB-based) and late-universe (local distance ladder) measurements of the Hubble constant, by introducing a new early dark energy model.
AI.method: Proposes an early dark energy model whose potential possesses an inverse power-law asymptotic tail, fitted to combined cosmological datasets (CMB+BAO+SN+H0DN).
AI.result: The model yields H0 = 70.20 (+0.60/-0.47) km/s/Mpc at 68% confidence (best-fit 70.56 km/s/Mpc) for index n=10, which helps alleviate the Hubble tension.
AI.conclusion: The model is testable with future CMB and matter power spectrum data, though fine-tuning issues associated with the model are briefly discussed.

title: COSMOS-Web: From early star-formation enhancement to late suppression in galaxy groups
summary: Galaxy groups trace dense environments where interactions, gas removal, and reduced accretion may drive quenching. Common diagnostics trace star formation over short timescales ($\lesssim 100$ Myr), so time-resolved star formation histories (SFHs) are needed to separate brief changes from longer-term evolution at fixed mass and redshift. Using COSMOS-Web data, we test how group environment correlates with star formation, how this evolves with cosmic time and group-centric distance, and how high-richness group galaxies differ from field galaxies. We combine COSMOS2025/COSMOS-Web stellar masses and non-parametric SFHs with AMICO group detections and probabilistic memberships. Using stacked SFHs and evolution diagnostics, we compare group and matched field galaxies as a function of normalized group-centric distance ($R_{\rm norm}$), using the richest groups as reference. The clearest suppression appears at $z<1.5$ and low-to-intermediate mass ($8.1<\log(M_\star/M_\odot)<10.5$), reaching a group-field SFH deficit up to 0.8 dex. At $z>1.5$, SFHs show weak suppression or occasional enhancement, a more heterogeneous contrast despite possible systematics. The radial signal also evolves: low-redshift profiles are broadly quenching-oriented across radius, while a clear inner-outer contrast emerges at $z\gtrsim 1$, though ordering at $z\gtrsim 2$ remains tentative given growing uncertainty in AMICO centroids. These results suggest an evolving picture: at early epochs groups are more mixed, with both suppressed and elevated SFHs; from $z\lesssim 1.5$, suppression dominates, most clearly for low-to-intermediate-mass galaxies. This fits inner-region galaxies spending more time within the group potential, undergoing more passages through dense intra-group regions, and receiving less pristine cold gas, making quenching progressively clearer with cosmic time.

AI.tldr: Using COSMOS-Web data, the paper combines stellar masses, non-parametric SFHs, and AMICO group memberships to compare stacked SFHs of group versus matched field galaxies across redshift and group-centric distance. It finds clear suppression at z<1.5 for low-to-intermediate mass galaxies (up to 0.8 dex deficit), weak or mixed effects at z>1.5, and a radial signal that becomes quenching-oriented at low redshift with inner-outer contrast emerging at z≳1, suggesting groups grow progressively more efficient at quenching with cosmic time.
AI.motivation: Common star formation diagnostics trace only short timescales (~100 Myr), so time-resolved SFHs are needed to distinguish brief bursts from long-term evolution in group environments. The paper seeks to understand how group environment correlates with star formation, how this evolves with cosmic time and group-centric distance, and how high-richness group galaxies differ from field galaxies at fixed mass and redshift.
AI.method: The analysis combines COSMOS2025/COSMOS-Web stellar masses and non-parametric SFHs with AMICO group detections and probabilistic memberships. Stacked SFHs and evolution diagnostics are used to compare group galaxies with matched field galaxies as a function of normalized group-centric distance (R_norm), using the richest groups as reference.
AI.result: The clearest SFH suppression appears at z<1.5 and low-to-intermediate mass (8.1<log(M*/Msun)<10.5), with a group-field deficit up to 0.8 dex. At z>1.5, suppression is weak or sometimes enhanced, giving a heterogeneous contrast. Radial profiles are broadly quenching-oriented across radius at low redshift, while an inner-outer contrast emerges at z≳1, though ordering at z≳2 remains tentative due to AMICO centroid uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: Results suggest an evolving picture: at early epochs groups are mixed environments with both suppressed and elevated star formation; from z≲1.5 suppression dominates, most clearly for low-to-intermediate-mass galaxies. This is consistent with inner-region galaxies spending more time in the group potential, undergoing more passages through dense intra-group regions, and receiving less pristine cold gas, making quenching progressively clearer with cosmic time.

title: Approximating the peculiar velocity distribution of dark matter halos with Tsallis statistics
summary: Dark matter halos, which host galaxies and galaxy clusters, have peculiar velocities far from thermal equilibrium. Characterizing the nonlinear and non-Gaussian features of this velocity distribution improves our understanding of the gravitational evolution of the cosmic web and supports related cosmological applications. We endeavor to establish a connection between the peculiar velocity distribution of halos and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, with the objective of obtaining a model that is both concise and accurate for practical applications. We extracted halo samples from large N-body simulations and performed maximum-likelihood fits to the peculiar velocity distributions using a two-parameter Tsallis model, derived from non-extensive statistical mechanics. On the theoretical side, we reformulated the halo distribution in the superstatistics framework by means of a generalized Gram-Charlier expansion based on the gamma distribution. For halo peculiar velocities below 1000 km/s, the Tsallis model achieves 5 percent accuracy over z=0-2, with performance improving toward lower redshifts. Our results show that the halo velocity distribution becomes increasingly non-Gaussian and departs further from equilibrium over time. The best-fit parameters depend only weakly on mass, though low-mass halos exhibit slightly stronger non-Gaussianity. The two parameters, especially the velocity dispersion, offer promising probes of cosmological parameters. Theoretically, we find that in general the halo peculiar velocity distribution function is expressible as a superposition of a series of Tsallis distribution functions, while simulation results demonstrate that the zeroth-order approximation, namely a single Tsallis function, already achieves sufficient accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper connects the peculiar velocity distribution of dark matter halos to nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, proposing a two-parameter Tsallis model derived from non-extensive statistical mechanics. The model achieves 5% accuracy for halo peculiar velocities below 1000 km/s over z=0-2, with performance improving toward lower redshifts. The velocity distribution becomes increasingly non-Gaussian over time, and the best-fit parameters offer promising probes of cosmological parameters.
AI.motivation: Dark matter halos have peculiar velocities far from thermal equilibrium, and characterizing their nonlinear and non-Gaussian features improves understanding of gravitational evolution of the cosmic web and supports cosmological applications. The goal is to establish a connection between halo peculiar velocity distributions and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics to obtain a concise yet accurate model for practical use.
AI.method: Halo samples are extracted from large N-body simulations, and maximum-likelihood fits to peculiar velocity distributions are performed using a two-parameter Tsallis model from non-extensive statistical mechanics. Theoretically, the halo distribution is reformulated within a superstatistics framework via a generalized Gram-Charlier expansion based on the gamma distribution.
AI.result: The Tsallis model achieves 5% accuracy for halo peculiar velocities below 1000 km/s over z=0-2, improving toward lower redshifts. Halo velocity distributions become increasingly non-Gaussian and depart further from equilibrium over time. Best-fit parameters depend only weakly on mass, though low-mass halos exhibit slightly stronger non-Gaussianity. The two parameters, especially velocity dispersion, offer promising cosmological probes. Theoretically, the halo peculiar velocity distribution is a superposition of Tsallis distribution functions, with the zeroth-order (single Tsallis function) approximation already providing sufficient accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The Tsallis model provides a concise and accurate description of halo peculiar velocity distributions, and the theoretical superstatistics reformulation confirms that a single Tsallis function serves as a sufficient zeroth-order approximation. The parameters, particularly velocity dispersion, are promising cosmological probes.

title: Systematic uncertainties on DESI Tully-Fisher distances constrained with Integral Field Spectroscopy
summary:
The Tully--Fisher (TF) relation is an empirical tool for estimating distances to spiral galaxies. The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Peculiar Velocity (PV) Survey uses \texttt{`tractor'} photometric position angles to place fibers along the galaxy's semi-major axis and infer maximum rotational velocities for $\approx$ 53,000 spirals. Systematic errors arise if the photometric PA differs from the kinematic PA from velocity fields.
  We quantify systematic uncertainties in DESI-TF distance estimates from photometric PAs and assess the impact of photometric--kinematic PA misalignments.
  We analyze 215 nearby galaxies from the PISCO and AMUSING surveys, estimating maximum rotational velocities at $0.4\,R_{26}$ for consistency with DESI-PV. Kinematic parameters are derived using \texttt{`PaFit'} from \texttt{`Cappellari Software'}. Global photometric parameters rely on Siena Galaxy Atlas SGA-2020 \texttt{`tractor'} data, with \texttt{`HostPhot'} as an alternative approach.
  Approximately $28\%$ of our sample exhibit photometric--kinematic PA misalignments $>10^\circ$. The median bias in distance is $\approx +1.98\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ with a skewed residual distribution of outliers. The overall distance standard deviation is $19.35\,\mathrm{Mpc}$, with misaligned galaxies showing twice the dispersion of aligned ones. The Mean Percentage Error is $2.8\% \pm 1.96$ (SE).
  High galaxy-to-galaxy scatter appears in DESI-TF distances, particularly for misaligned systems. Because DESI-TF targets lack kinematic PA measurements, we recommend a global fractional uncertainty of $\approx 3.5\%$. When kinematic information is available, aligned galaxies with offsets $<10^\circ$ are consistent with $\approx 1\%$ uncertainty, while strongly misaligned or incomplete systems warrant an upper threshold of $\approx 10\%$.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies systematic uncertainties in DESI Tully-Fisher (TF) distance estimates arising from photometric position angle (PA) versus kinematic PA misalignments. Analyzing 215 nearby galaxies, ~28% show misalignments >10°, leading to median distance bias of ~1.98 Mpc, overall distance scatter of 19.35 Mpc, and ~3.5% recommended global fractional uncertainty for DESI-TF targets lacking kinematic PA information.
AI.motivation: The DESI Peculiar Velocity Survey uses photometric position angles from 'tractor' data to place fibers along spiral galaxy semi-major axes and infer rotational velocities for ~53,000 galaxies. If the photometric PA differs from the true kinematic PA, systematic errors in TF-based distance estimates arise. This work aims to quantify these systematic uncertainties and assess the impact of PA misalignment on distance accuracy.
AI.method: The study analyzes 215 nearby galaxies from the PISCO and AMUSING surveys. Maximum rotational velocities are estimated at 0.4 R26 to match DESI-PV conventions, using the 'PaFit' kinematic fitting software. Global photometric parameters are derived from Siena Galaxy Atlas SGA-2020 'tractor' data, with 'HostPhot' used as an alternative. Photometric-kinematic PA misalignments are computed and their effect on TF distances is statistically characterized.
AI.result: Approximately 28% of the sample exhibits photometric-kinematic PA misalignments >10°. The median distance bias is ~+1.98 Mpc with a skewed outlier residual distribution. Overall distance standard deviation is 19.35 Mpc, with misaligned galaxies showing twice the dispersion of aligned ones. The Mean Percentage Error is 2.8% ± 1.96 (SE). Aligned galaxies (offset <10°) are consistent with ~1% uncertainty, while strongly misaligned or incomplete systems warrant an upper threshold of ~10%.
AI.conclusion: High galaxy-to-galaxy scatter appears in DESI-TF distances, particularly for misaligned systems. Since DESI-TF targets lack kinematic PA measurements, a global fractional uncertainty of ~3.5% is recommended for these distance estimates. When kinematic information is available, the uncertainty can be reduced to ~1% for aligned systems, while strongly misaligned or incomplete systems require a conservative ≥10% uncertainty.

title: ELUCID-DESI II. Revealing dark matter mass, tidal, and velocity (MTV) fields using galaxy group phase information
summary: We introduce a novel method for reconstructing the cosmic mass, tidal, and velocity (MTV) fields over the redshift range $0 < z < 0.6$ using the phase information of galaxy groups. This approach replaces the explicit theoretical bias correction typically needed to relate galaxy groups to the underlying dark matter density field with a simulation-calibrated statistical mapping, reducing a major source of systematic uncertainty and making the method directly applicable to spectroscopic redshift surveys such as the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS). We evaluate the performance of our MTV reconstruction pipeline with mock redshift surveys that include a comprehensive set of observational selection effects. The galaxy groups used as tracers are identified with an extended halo-based group finder applied to the DESI mock galaxy catalogue with an apparent magnitude limit of $m_z < 19.65$, yielding a galaxy number comparable to that of the DESI BGS faint sample ($m_r < 20.175$). Our tests show that the reconstructed velocities are accurate and unbiased, with a residual dispersion of $\sim 120\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ across the redshift bins. The recovered velocity field allows us to shift galaxy groups to their real-space positions, thereby correcting for the Kaiser effect. By iteratively applying this Kaiser correction to the galaxy groups, we further reconstruct the tidal field and the mass-density distribution. The reconstruction is stable with respect to the grid resolution. Overall, our results demonstrate that this group-based phase-space reconstruction provides a robust pathway to recovering the dark matter MTV fields, with strong prospects for application to DESI BGS data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a novel method for reconstructing the cosmic mass, tidal, and velocity (MTV) fields over 0 < z < 0.6 using the phase information of galaxy groups, replacing explicit theoretical bias correction with a simulation-calibrated statistical mapping. Tested on mock DESI BGS-like catalogs, the method recovers unbiased velocities with ~120 km/s residual dispersion, corrects the Kaiser effect by shifting groups to real-space positions, and iteratively reconstructs the tidal and mass-density fields.
AI.motivation: Traditional reconstruction of dark matter density fields requires explicit theoretical bias corrections to relate galaxy groups to the underlying matter distribution, introducing major systematic uncertainties. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency and make reconstruction directly applicable to large spectroscopic redshift surveys like the DESI BGS.
AI.method: The method uses phase information of galaxy groups identified via an extended halo-based group finder applied to a DESI mock galaxy catalog (m_z < 19.65). It employs a simulation-calibrated statistical mapping instead of explicit bias corrections. The pipeline iteratively applies Kaiser correction—shifting galaxy groups from redshift-space to real-space positions using the reconstructed velocity field—to recover the velocity, tidal, and mass-density fields.
AI.result: Reconstructed velocities are accurate and unbiased with residual dispersion of ~120 km/s across redshift bins. The recovered velocity field corrects the Kaiser effect by moving groups to real-space positions. Iterative Kaiser correction enables successful tidal field and mass-density reconstruction, stable with respect to grid resolution.
AI.conclusion: The group-based phase-space MTV reconstruction provides a robust pathway to recovering dark matter mass, tidal, and velocity fields with strong prospects for application to DESI BGS data.

title: A radio continuum view of Stephan's Quintet: age, dynamics and origin of the shock
comment: 25 pages, 13 Figures, Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We present a detailed, multi-band radio continuum study of the compact galaxy group Stephan's Quintet (HCG 92). We use a combination of new (MeerKAT, uGMRT) and archival (LOFAR, VLA) observations covering the $\rm 120\,MHz{-}8\,GHz$ frequency range to examine the radio properties of the group, focusing on the famous radio ridge and surrounding diffuse emission. We find filamentary substructure and branching in the southern half of the ridge, confirm an extension of the ridge to the northwest, and identify for the first time a radio counterpart to the gas bridge linking the ridge and NGC 7319. The northern ridge, northwest extension and diffuse emission have relatively steep, curved spectra, with a high-frequency spectral index gradient running north-south along the ridge. We show that the ridge emission primarily arises from a single physical mechanism, probably strong ($\mathcal{M}\simeq 40-100$) shocks in cold gas, caused by the $\rm \sim850-1000\,kms^{-1}$ collision between NGC 7318B and tidal gas filaments produced by past galaxy interactions. Synchrotron spectral age estimates suggest the collision began at the north end of the ridge $\rm \sim20\,Myr$ ago, and finished only $\rm \sim5-6\,Myr$ ago in the south, with the southern end of the shocked ridge likely still within or close to the disk of NGC 7318B. Based on this age gradient, we find that the angle between the intruder galaxy's motion and the tidal filaments was probably only about 15 degrees, and combining this with the lack of a spectral index gradient in the diffuse radio emission suggests that NGC 7318B's direction of motion is probably close to the line of sight.

AI.tldr: A multi-band radio study (120 MHz–8 GHz) of Stephan's Quintet using MeerKAT, uGMRT, LOFAR, and VLA data reveals detailed substructure in the radio ridge, including filaments, a northwest extension, and a newly discovered radio counterpart to the gas bridge. The ridge arises from strong shocks (Mach 40–100) caused by the high-velocity collision of NGC 7318B with tidal gas filaments, with spectral ages indicating the collision progressed from north (~20 Myr ago) to south (~5–6 Myr ago), implying a shallow incidence angle of ~15° and near-line-of-sight motion of the intruder.
AI.motivation: To provide a detailed, high-resolution multi-band radio continuum study of the compact galaxy group Stephan's Quintet, focusing on the famous radio ridge and surrounding diffuse emission to understand their physical origin and the dynamics of the ongoing galaxy collision.
AI.method: Combining new MeerKAT and uGMRT observations with archival LOFAR and VLA data spanning 120 MHz–8 GHz, the authors perform a multi-band radio continuum analysis, examine spectral indices and curvature, and apply synchrotron spectral age modeling to the ridge emission.
AI.result: The study finds filamentary substructure and branching in the southern ridge, confirms a northwest extension, and identifies a new radio counterpart to the gas bridge. The emission shows steep, curved spectra with a north-south spectral index gradient along the ridge. The ridge is attributed to strong shocks (Mach ~40–100) from the ~850–1000 km/s collision of NGC 7318B with tidal gas filaments. Spectral ages indicate the collision began ~20 Myr ago in the north and finished ~5–6 Myr ago in the south, implying a ~15° angle between the intruder's motion and the filaments, with motion likely near the line of sight.
AI.conclusion: The radio ridge in Stephan's Quintet is produced by a single physical mechanism—strong shocks in cold gas from the collision of NGC 7318B with tidal filaments—with an age gradient revealing the progression of the collision from north to south and constraining the intruder's orbital geometry to a shallow incidence angle with near-line-of-sight motion.

title: Derivative hierarchy as the origin of kernel-dependent trends in Gaussian process reconstructions of the hubble parameter
summary: We perform a model independent reconstruction of the cosmic expansion history using Gaussian Process regression, investigating how the smoothness properties of covariance kernels influence the inferred Hubble parameter. Using 32 cosmic chronometer measurements, we reconstruct $H(z)$ with the Matérn $3/2$, $5/2$, $7/2$, $9/2$, and Squared Exponential kernels, which form a well-defined hierarchy of differentiability. Across this hierarchy, we observe a systematic and monotonic trend in which increasing kernel smoothness is associated with progressively lower reconstructed values of the present-day Hubble constant $H_0$, accompanied by reduced statistical uncertainties. Rather than indicating a statistical preference for a specific kernel, this behaviour reflects the sensitivity of non-parametric reconstructions to the assumed smoothness prior encoded in the covariance function. The same ordering is reflected in descriptive goodness-of-fit statistics and remains stable when incorporating recent DESI DR2 BAO measurements and performing jackknife resampling tests, demonstrating robustness against individual data points and dataset variations. Additional analysis of derivative reconstructions shows that differences in kernel differentiability propagate into the local slope of the expansion history, providing a consistent interpretation of the observed ordering in $H_0$. Our results highlight that kernel smoothness plays an important role in Gaussian Process reconstructions and should be carefully accounted for when interpreting non-parametric cosmological inferences.

AI.tldr: This paper performs a model-independent reconstruction of the cosmic expansion history H(z) using Gaussian Process regression with 32 cosmic chronometer measurements, systematically testing a hierarchy of covariance kernels (Matérn 3/2 through 9/2 and Squared Exponential). The authors find a monotonic trend where increasing kernel smoothness yields lower reconstructed H0 values with reduced uncertainties, reflecting the sensitivity of non-parametric reconstructions to the assumed smoothness prior rather than statistical preference. This ordering persists with DESI DR2 BAO data and jackknife tests, and propagates into derivative reconstructions of the expansion history.
AI.motivation: Non-parametric reconstructions of cosmic expansion depend on prior assumptions encoded in the covariance kernel, yet the systematic impact of kernel smoothness on inferred cosmological parameters like H0 has not been carefully quantified. Understanding this sensitivity is crucial for correctly interpreting model-independent cosmological inferences.
AI.method: Gaussian Process regression is applied to 32 cosmic chronometer measurements to reconstruct H(z). Five covariance kernels forming a strict differentiability hierarchy (Matérn 3/2, 5/2, 7/2, 9/2, and Squared Exponential) are tested. Robustness is assessed by adding DESI DR2 BAO data and performing jackknife resampling. Derivative reconstructions are also analyzed to trace how kernel smoothness propagates into the slope of the expansion history.
AI.result: A systematic and monotonic trend is found: increasing kernel smoothness leads to progressively lower reconstructed H0 values with smaller statistical uncertainties. This ordering is stable when incorporating DESI DR2 BAO data and under jackknife resampling. The same ordering appears in descriptive goodness-of-fit statistics and propagates into the derivative of the expansion history.
AI.conclusion: Kernel smoothness is a critical prior assumption in Gaussian Process reconstructions of the cosmic expansion history. The observed kernel-induced ordering in H0 is not evidence for any particular kernel but rather demonstrates that non-parametric inferences are sensitive to the smoothness prior. This should be carefully accounted for when interpreting model-independent cosmological results.

title: Visualizing Disequilibrium: Tracing Two-Point Correlations to Specific Spatial Structures in the Milky Way
comment: Published in the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: The Two-Point Correlation Function can be used to demonstrate the existence of substructure within a dataset, but typical implementations do not track the individual points which contribute to each specific substructure. In this paper, we develop an algorithm that traces a two-point correlation signal back to the contributions of each data point, allowing for structure to be visualized in novel ways. Using this tool, we find substantial evidence for pervasive spatial clustering in the Milky Way and reveal complex undulations that warp the previously discovered vertical density waves. We also explore the ``clumping" of stars in the thick disk and near-halo regions and discuss the possibility of dating the structure.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an algorithm that traces two-point correlation function signals back to the contributions of individual data points, enabling novel visualization of substructure. The method reveals pervasive spatial clustering in the Milky Way, complex undulations in vertical density waves, and clumping of stars in the thick disk and near-halo regions, with potential for dating structures.
AI.motivation: Typical implementations of the Two-Point Correlation Function demonstrate substructure in datasets but do not track which individual points contribute to each specific substructure, limiting the ability to visualize and analyze the underlying structure.
AI.method: The algorithm traces a two-point correlation signal back to the per-point contributions, allowing each data point's role in the global correlation structure to be identified and visualized directly.
AI.result: The tool finds substantial evidence for pervasive spatial clustering in the Milky Way, uncovers complex undulations warping previously discovered vertical density waves, and reveals clumping of stars in the thick disk and near-halo regions.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables novel visualization of correlation-based substructure and opens the possibility of dating structures within the data, offering new insights into Milky Way morphology.

title: Bumpy inflation from explosive particle production
summary: We present a first-principles derivation of an effective inflaton potential with a bumpy feature. We consider the coupling of a spectator field χto the inflaton φsuch that χis massive enough for almost all values of φ, but becomes massless when the inflaton crossed the value φ_\star. This gives rise to a burst of χ-particle production at φ=φ_\star. By taking the backreaction of the particle production, we obtain a bumpy feature in the effective potential.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an effective inflaton potential with a bumpy feature from first principles by coupling the inflaton to a spectator field that transiently becomes massless at a specific field value, causing particle production whose backreaction generates the bump.
AI.motivation: To provide a first-principles derivation of a bumpy feature in the inflaton effective potential, rather than parametrizing it ad hoc, by showing how a spectator field coupling can naturally generate such a feature through particle production.
AI.method: The inflaton φ is coupled to a spectator field χ such that χ becomes massless only when φ crosses the value φ★. This triggers a burst of χ-particle production at that point. The backreaction of this particle production is then computed to obtain the effective inflaton potential with a bumpy feature.
AI.result: A bumpy feature in the effective inflaton potential is obtained as a result of the backreaction from the burst of χ-particle production occurring when the spectator field becomes massless at φ = φ★.
AI.conclusion: Spectator field couplings that induce temporary masslessness and associated particle production provide a physical and first-principles mechanism for generating bumpy features in the inflaton potential.

title: SERENADE III: Insight into the Origin of the High Dust Temperature and High [O III]/[C II] Ratio at $z\gtrsim6$
summary: We present an analysis of ALMA high-frequency observations of nine bright Lyman-break galaxies at $5.8<z_{\rm spec}<8.3$. Our sample consists of five galaxies at $z\sim6$ newly observed in Band-9 and/or 10, allowing us to better constrain the dust temperature ($T_{\rm dust}$) in a statistical sample of $z\gtrsim6$ galaxies. Our measurements of the dust temperature at $z\sim6-9$ suggest most of the star-forming galaxies show $T_{\rm dust}\sim40\,{\rm K}$ on average, whereas three galaxies show significantly higher $T_{\rm dust}$ ($\gtrsim60\,{\rm K}$).
